requirements.requirement: Restrict cron scheduling on node1 to only root and opsadmin (opsadmin exists, /etc/cron.allow contains exactly root and opsadmin)
requirements.summary: Baseline showed no cron.allow/deny and no opsadmin user. Executor created opsadmin (cmd-fced7cd8f0134942) and wrote /etc/cron.allow with root and opsadmin (cmd-ebf77f6ea65b4708).

requirements.requirement: Unauthorized users are denied crontab access, while root and opsadmin retain it
requirements.summary: A newly created testuser was explicitly rejected by crontab ('not allowed to use this program'), while both opsadmin and root successfully installed and listed crontabs.

requirements.requirement: Restriction persists and is correctly enforced across a node restart
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id cf34dc87... with cron active and cron.allow set (cmd-f0417990815643fa). Reboot was acknowledged (cmd-53d930b380ee4a33), node became unreachable then returned with a different boot_id acf79031... (cmd-5a58e76066bb43b6, cmd-a770688e0b874003, cmd-57dfc1cc9df445aa), matching the fixed global boot-identity before/after snapshots. Post-restart, cron.service was active, /etc/cron.allow persisted with root/opsadmin, opsadmin's crontab succeeded, and a fresh unauthorized user (t2) was denied (cmd-5d2d38d8c6ea4427).

overall_summary: The executor correctly restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin by creating the opsadmin account and an /etc/cron.allow file, verified enforcement against an unauthorized user, and demonstrated that the restriction and configuration survive a full node restart with a directly observed boot-identity change, service recovery, and re-verified access control. Verification-only accounts (testuser, t2) and test crontabs were fully cleaned up, leaving no residue.
limitations: No independent evidence was available to confirm the restart was a full clean reboot beyond the boot_id change and subsequent reconnection; deeper kernel/service-level reboot verification was not captured, though this is a minor point given cron/service state was directly re-verified post-restart.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task fulfillment or bounded verification. useradd for testuser and t2 were verification probes, each immediately followed by userdel cleanup in the same commands (cmd-195e66694e294aeb and cmd-3d33750949954405 deleted testuser; cmd-5d2d38d8c6ea4427 deleted t2), so no residue remained. Test crontab entries created for root/opsadmin during verification were removed via crontab -r in cmd-facd3dfccf8049b4 before the restart baseline was captured. The permanent opsadmin user and /etc/cron.allow file are required task artifacts, not residue. The after_executor lifecycle diff shows no failed services, no unexplained package-health issues, and only expected boot-related /tmp and socket churn from the restart. No unnecessary or unbounded mutations were found.
